title: How hot and how cold does your town get?
description: A thermometer scale with zero marked as the freezing point of water, and two readings placed on it, one above zero and one that could fall below. The video shows how a reading gets its sign, and Keeko's doubt that every winter reading is below zero is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: a reading is positive above zero and negative below zero, and cold weather alone does not make it negative. Watch for students who think every winter reading is a negative number.

source: What has been the maximum temperature during the summer and
video_script.why: The child finds the hottest summer reading and the coldest winter reading of their own area and learns that zero degrees Celsius is the line between positive and negative readings.
video_script.substitution: The book's own two thermometers, forty and fifteen degrees Celsius, stand for the readings the child looks up.
video_script.anchor: the thermometer of the book, with a scale in degrees Celsius that carries on below zero
video_script.wrong_answer: every winter reading is below zero
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks every winter reading is below zero because winter is cold. The book says only some places in India go below zero, and a cool reading such as fifteen degrees Celsius is still above zero.
video_script.payoff_line: A reading is negative only when it is below zero.

final_answer.value: Your own two readings, each placed above or below 0 °C
final_answer.spoken: your own two readings, each placed above or below zero

hold_back: Your own two readings, each placed above or below 0 °C
maths_rules: 0 °C is the freezing point of water
a reading above 0 °C is a positive number; a reading below 0 °C is a negative number
the book's thermometers show 40 °C and 15 °C; both are above 0 °C, so both are positive
the answer is a local fact the child looks up, so the video gives no fixed value
video_script.design: One thermometer scale in degrees Celsius with zero marked. Teal above zero for positive, amber below zero for negative. The book's two readings sit above zero; a dotted marker below zero shows where a very cold place would be.
open_questions: The book asks for a local fact to look up, so the answer is the method of placing each reading against zero, not one number.
